subject: physiology
title: Regional circulation, shock and exercise

steps.tx: Coronary flow is set mainly by **local arteriolar vasodilation** in response to myocardial oxygen need. Falling oxygen tension leads to breakdown of ATP, release of **adenosine**, and vasodilation. Coronary flow is largely driven by the pressure gradient, and it is squeezed during systole in the left ventricle. Flow is therefore greatest in diastole on the left, whereas on the right it peaks in systole.

steps.tx: Myocardial **oxygen demand** is set by the work of the heart. It rises with heart rate, contractility, afterload, preload and intramyocardial tension, and falls with greater wall thickness. Haemoglobin concentration affects oxygen supply rather than demand. In exam questions, tachycardia and raised afterload are the classic reasons for ischaemia when supply cannot keep pace.

vis.alt: Balance of myocardial oxygen: demand rises with heart rate, contractility, wall tension from preload and afterload; supply depends on diastolic aortic pressure, coronary vascular resistance, diastolic time and oxygen content; extraction is already about 70 percent so extra demand must be met by flow.
vis.caption: Tachycardia hurts twice: demand rises and diastole, when the left ventricle is perfused, shortens.

steps.tx: In **haemorrhagic shock**, sympathetic activity compensates for falling venous return. Generalised vasoconstriction raises total peripheral resistance, heart rate and contractility rise, and renin release retains sodium and water. Fluid also shifts from the interstitial and intracellular spaces into the vessels. Respiratory rate increases too, so the compensatory response is a rise in heart rate, not a fall.

left.title: Compensatory responses
points: Renin release, sodium and water retention

steps.tx: During **exercise**, sympathetic drive raises heart rate and stroke volume, so cardiac output rises mainly through heart rate. Mean arterial pressure rises, while diastolic pressure stays flat or falls. Active muscle flow can increase about 25-fold, with metabolites such as potassium and adenosine causing vasodilation. Splanchnic, renal and inactive muscle flow fall, while cerebral flow stays essentially unchanged.

steps.tx: On **standing**, about 300 to 500 mL of blood pools in the leg veins, reducing venous return and cardiac output. Baroreceptor unloading raises sympathetic tone, so heart rate and peripheral resistance increase. Syncope and **postural hypotension** occur when this reflex fails. On lying down, blood returns from the legs, and pulmonary blood volume can rise by up to 400 mL, which is why orthopnoea appears in heart failure.

vis.alt: Response to standing: 300 to 500 mL of blood pools in the leg veins, venous return and cardiac output fall, baroreceptor unloading raises sympathetic tone and lowers vagal tone, heart rate and vasoconstriction restore pressure; failure causes orthostatic hypotension.
vis.caption: Standing pools blood in the legs; the baroreflex restores pressure within seconds.
